clue.text: Preening female at work, half high on heroin

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece on another comes before it

parts.note: OP is short for operating, so at work

indicators.note: only half the letters of the high word are kept

parts.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, so high on drink
H is drug slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A vain woman at the office is half out of it on heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: PISSED loses its second half SED, leaving PIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Foppish means vain and dandified, which fits someone who is preening.

clue.text: Reckon a sexual act produces a crafty bust?

parts.note: to figure is to reckon or work out
HEAD is slang for oral sex

explanation.surface: Someone boasting that a sex act can be passed off as a clever police raid.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants a bust by the police; the setter means a carved torso, and 'crafty' is the craft it rides on.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurehead is the carved bust on a ship's prow, so it is a bust belonging to a craft — 'crafty' in a punning sense.

clue.text: Screwed in a dividing copper flap

indicators.note: the jumbled letters divide the copper's letters by sitting between them

parts.note: PC is a police constable, and a copper is a policeman

indicators.note: screwed means twisted, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A twisted copper strip splits a flap open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like the metal; it is a British police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Flap is informal for a state of agitated alarm, so it means panic.

clue.text: Entering office being elected, then resigning

indicators.note: 'then' means next in sequence, so the second piece follows the first

parts.note: a candidate who is elected gets IN
someone resigning is going

explanation.surface: A politician's whole career in five words: elected, then quitting.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a short-lived minister; the definition sits in the first two words, and the rest builds the word from its two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingoing means coming in, as of an incoming officeholder entering a post.

clue.text: Tool covers Private Eye, though shrunken? Respect!

indicators.note: covers means surrounds, so the tool's letters go round the rest

parts.note: a hoe is a garden tool

indicators.note: the word for the publication is cut down to its short form

parts.note: Private Eye is a British satirical magazine

explanation.surface: A tool covering a shrunken Private Eye deserves some respect.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye is the British satirical fortnightly that runs this puzzle, so it stands for its type of publication.
explanation.definitionFit: Homage is public honour or tribute, a show of respect.

clue.text: Arm-raisers with an "either sex OK" attitude, against Anglican Church's taking power?

indicators.note: 'against' means right up next to, so the pieces are placed side by side

parts.note: BI is short for bisexual, attracted to either sex

indicators.note: a word taking something takes it into itself, so that letter goes inside

parts.note: CE is the Church of England, with the 's kept as S
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: Liberal protesters with their hands up, raised against the Church of England's grab for power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arm-raisers' reads like demonstrators with their fists up; it is the muscles that do the raising. The power letter sits between the church and its apostrophe S.
explanation.definitionFit: The biceps is the muscle at the front of the upper arm that bends the elbow and lifts the forearm, so biceps are literally arm-raisers.

clue.text: Greater London area nuts

definitions.meaning: a district in the east of the capital, sharing a borough with Dagenham
British slang for mad, often followed by the word 'mad' itself

explanation.surface: A remark that some part of Greater London is mad.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the place name and the slang for madness are the same word, so the surface's insult is also the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Barking is a district of the London Borough of Barking and Dagenham, and 'barking' is British slang for mad, as in 'barking mad'.

clue.text: Small business worried mostly about ring procedure to divert motions

parts.note: CO is short for company, a business

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go about the ring, enclosing it
worried means agitated, so the letters are shaken up

parts.note: O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A small firm worries about a ring-shaped bowel operation.
explanation.walkthrough: MOSTLY is reordered to LOSTMY with O placed after LOST.
explanation.definitionFit: A colostomy diverts the colon through the abdomen into a bag, rerouting bowel motions.

clue.text: Depression hits tense prime minister

parts.note: a pit is a hollow or depression in the ground
T is the grammarians' abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A prime minister struck down by depression at a tense time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' pretends to be a mood; it is a hole in the ground. Either Pitt, the Elder or the Younger, will do.
explanation.definitionFit: William Pitt the Elder and his son William Pitt the Younger were both British prime ministers in the eighteenth century.

clue.text: Hot drink no good after turkey, potentially

indicators.note: in an across entry, a piece placed after another comes behind it, so the second-named piece goes first

parts.note: an egg is a turkey that has not hatched yet
NO plus G, the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Grumbling that the hot drink was no good after Christmas turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turkey' sets up a Christmas dinner, where eggnog belongs; 'potentially' turns the bird into what it might hatch from.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggnog is a drink of beaten eggs, milk, sugar and often spirits, served warm or cold, especially at Christmas.

clue.text: Liam mucked about with Tory honesty and integrity?

indicators.note: things mucked about are messed around with, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: fodder taken as written
fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A Tory called Liam — Liam Fox, the Conservative defence secretary who resigned in 2011 — messing about with honesty and integrity.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark lets the setter pair Tory scandal with a definition by example: honesty and integrity are two kinds of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Morality is principled conduct, of which honesty and integrity are examples, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Inflicting torture during wanks: rather controversial means of releasing gas

definitions.text: rather controversial means of releasing gas

indicators.note: something going on during another thing happens in the middle of it, so it goes inside

parts.note: FRIG is British slang for masturbate
to rack is to torture someone on the rack

explanation.surface: A lurid mix of torture and self-abuse, followed by a coy remark about letting out wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Releasing gas' pretends to be the schoolboy joke that 'wanks' sets up; it means extracting shale gas. The torture goes in just after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Fracking rigs pump fluid into shale to crack it and release natural gas, a practice that has been bitterly contested in Britain.

clue.text: Maybe Cameron produced nation on dole, no getting away from it

indicators.note: letters produced are worked up into something new, so they are rearranged
letters getting away from the rest leave them, so they are removed

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written
the two letters that leave before the rearranging

explanation.surface: A gibe that an Etonian prime minister has put the whole country on benefits, and there is no escaping it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks David Cameron as one example: he was educated at Eton. 'No getting away from it' sounds like a shrug, but it tells two letters to leave the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An Old Etonian is a former pupil of Eton College, and David Cameron, prime minister from 2010, is one, hence 'Maybe'.

clue.text: Hosts require minimal coverage by Sun about Rupert's introduction

indicators.note: a name's introduction is its opening, so only the first letter is used
'about' means surrounding, so the pieces wrap round the letter

parts.note: a thong is skimpy underwear or swimwear that covers very little
the first letter of Rupert
S is the abbreviation for Sunday; the Sun also puns on the tabloid

explanation.surface: Rupert Murdoch's Sun insisting its presenters wear skimpy outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hosts' sounds like presenters, matching the tabloid picture; it means crowds, as in heavenly hosts.
explanation.definitionFit: A host is a large number of people, as in 'a host of admirers', so hosts are throngs.

clue.text: Poetry in first third of Oxford edition — can't get enough of it

indicators.note: the poetry word goes in the Oxford letters

parts.note: Oxford has six letters, so its first third is the first two
verse is poetry

explanation.surface: Poetry in the first part of an Oxford edition leaves you wanting more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' in the definition is the usual coy word for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone oversexed has an excessive sex drive, so never has enough sex.

clue.text: Mean, on reflection, private peer

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror is back to front, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: a peer is a noble
a private soldier is a GI, reversed

explanation.surface: Someone thinking over what 'mean' means, and a peer taking a private look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' and 'peer' pretend to be about peeping; one is an American soldier and the other a member of the House of Lords.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignoble means base or dishonourable in character, which is one sense of 'mean'.

clue.text: Naked American pissed as a Serb

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: An American and a Serb out drinking, one of them stripped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American' pretends to be a person; it marks the answer as American slang. To a British reader 'pissed' means drunk; to an American, angry.
explanation.definitionFit: Bare-ass is American slang for completely naked, so 'naked American' is the US word for naked.

clue.text: He's smeared with balm to do a drag walk

indicators.note: something smeared has been smudged out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: fodder taken as written
fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A man plastering himself with balm before walking out in drag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drag' pretends to be women's clothes worn by a man; it means dragging the feet.
explanation.definitionFit: To shamble is to walk awkwardly, dragging the feet, so it is a walk that drags.

clue.text: Wallowing, yes, in dump presided over by the pope

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go in the dump word

parts.note: a hole is a dump, a squalid place

indicators.note: wallowing means rolling about, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Someone wallows in a dump, saying yes, ruled by the pope.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy See is the Roman Catholic jurisdiction of Rome, governed by the pope as its bishop.

clue.text: Roger, to an unacceptable degree, is veneer?

parts.note: 'over' means too much, as in overdone
to roger and to lay are both British slang for having sex

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone has had too much sex, and whether it is only on the surface.
explanation.walkthrough: The blocks are taken in the answer's order, the reverse of the clue's. 'Roger' pretends to be a name; it is British slang for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: A veneer is a thin surface layer laid over something else, which is an overlay; the question mark marks it as one example.

clue.text: Rising FBI agent gets put away for licking

indicators.note: in a down entry, a word rising reads from the bottom up, so it is reversed

parts.note: to put food away is to eat it
an FBI agent is a FED, reversed

explanation.surface: An up-and-coming FBI agent jailed for licking something he shouldn't.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' reads as jailed and 'licking' as a tongue job; it is eating and a thrashing.
explanation.definitionFit: A licking is a beating or a heavy defeat, as in 'the team took a licking'.

clue.text: Government handout, say, gets a holiday place abroad

parts.note: to say is to state
a pension is a boarding house or small hotel in continental Europe

explanation.surface: A pensioner spending the government handout on a holiday abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like a signal for an example, but it is a verb in its own right. The second word is the French pension, pronounced the continental way.
explanation.definitionFit: The state pension is the regular payment the British government makes to people above retirement age.

clue.text: Lean Jack Straw's prime dope

indicators.note: the prime part of something is its first, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of Straw
a prat is British slang for a fool or dope

explanation.surface: An insult calling Jack Straw, the Labour home secretary and foreign secretary, a skinny dope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack Straw' reads as the politician, but the definition takes 'Jack' away from him to stand with 'Lean'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme, 'Jack Sprat could eat no fat', so he is the lean Jack.

clue.text: Labour leader involved in rubbish idea

indicators.note: a thing involved in another is wrapped up inside it

parts.note: to pan something is to rubbish it

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its head

parts.note: the first letter of Labour

explanation.surface: A jab that the Labour leader has been caught up in a rubbish idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' pretends to be the party's head; it gives only the party's first letter. 'Rubbish' is the critic's verb, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea about what to do is a plan, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Feel bad about voter's choice: beaten Lib. yielding

indicators.note: about means the scrambled feel goes around what follows
something gone bad has been spoiled, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
a voter marks a choice with a cross, X

indicators.note: beaten means knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy Liberal Democrat feels let down by voters' verdict after a drubbing at the polls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feel bad' and 'beaten Lib.' are two separate anagrams; the voter's cross and the second scramble together sit inside the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flexible bends or gives way under pressure rather than resisting, so it is pliant.

clue.text: He did lines of heroin finally after frolic with Cyclops

indicators.note: a word's final part is its last letter
in an across entry, a piece placed after another comes behind it

parts.note: a lark is a bit of fun, a frolic
the setter's own name, standing for 'me', gives I
the last letter of heroin

explanation.surface: A man doing lines of heroin after a romp with Cyclops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' pretends to be drugs, and 'heroin' backs it up; they are lines of verse. A setter's name in the clue is the setter speaking, so it gives I.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Larkin was an English poet, so he wrote lines of verse.

clue.text: Feeling restless, done getting screwed? Say "turning over"

indicators.note: screwed means twisted, so the letters are rearranged
turning over says the abbreviation is read in the other direction

parts.note: EG, for example, is said before an instance, like say

explanation.surface: Someone feels anxious about being cheated and asks for a turnover.
explanation.walkthrough: DONE rearranges to ONED; EG for say turns to GE.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on edge is to be nervous and tense, unable to settle.

clue.text: Tory nit given a makeover — see just how far one can go?

definitions.text: see just how far one can go

indicators.note: a thing given a makeover is remodelled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A foolish Tory given a makeover, testing how far he can push it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makeover' fits the answer's other sense too: trying on new clothes. The definition is the British idiom for testing someone's patience.
explanation.definitionFit: To try it on, in British idiom, is to test how much you can get away with.
